text: Ἐλεύθερον. Ἐλεύθερος, liber, ingenuus, honestus, probus, ἐλευθέρα, libera, ingenua, honesta, matrona, uxor. Sic apud Cyrillum Alexandrinum, lib. VII Contra Julianum, p. 229 A: Ἐλευθέρα γυνιχί. Et τὴν εὔφυᾶ καὶ ἐλεύθερον, p. autem 244 D. Γάμων ἐλευθέρων λησταί. Occurritque ἐλευθέρας nomen sæpe in Basilio, Chrysostomo, Palladio, Moscho, aliisque; interdum vero imperitia librariorum evasit in ἐλευθερίαν, ut apud Chrysostomum non semel observarunt viri docti. Cui adde Basilium, epist. 188, cum Nostro cap. 188. Sed et puto Palladium in Dialogo de vita Chrysostomi, p. 155, scripsisse: Οὐ τῷ σκοπῷ τῆς ἐλευθέρας προσέχων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς Θεοφίλου θρύλλοις. Scopo probæ mulieris non attendens, sed Theophili fabulis. Loquitur de Olympiade, quamquam ἐλευθερίας retineri posset, atque exponi de libertate et liberalitate.
anchorLine: τητος εἰσελθόντος πρὸς τὸν ἐλεύθερον (t) κατὰ τὸ
en: ἐλεύθερον. Ἐλεύθερος means free, freeborn, honorable, upright; ἐλευθέρα, free woman, freeborn, honorable, matron, wife. So in Cyril of Alexandria, book 7 Against Julian, p. 229 A: 'a free woman'; and 'the well-born and free', and on p. 244 D 'robbers of free marriages'. The noun ἐλευθέρας occurs often in Basil, Chrysostom, Palladius, Moschus and others; sometimes through the ignorance of copyists it has slipped into ἐλευθερίαν, as learned men have noted more than once in Chrysostom. Add Basil, epistle 188, with our own chapter 188. And I think Palladius wrote in the Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom, p. 155: 'not heeding the aim of the free (noble) woman, but the tales of Theophilus', meaning heeding not the respectable woman's purpose but Theophilus's fables. He is speaking of Olympias, although ἐλευθερίας could be kept and be explained of freedom and generosity.

text: Περιοδευθῆναι. Ad quid explicarem verbum quod obscurum non est? Cur ergo Nota? Ut emendetur sancti Nili epistola 285, lib. II: Ἵνα γνῷς σαφέστατα καὶ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ τὴν μανίαν, καὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ τὴν κηδεμονίαν, θᾶττον περιοδεύσαντός σε, ὡς εὐνούστατον δοῦλον. Ut clarissime cognoscas et adversarii rabiem, et Christi sollicitudinem, qui te veluti servum dilectissimum quantocius curavit. Περιοδυνήσαντος; contrarium plane sensum reddit.
anchorLine: θεν εἰς πόλιν τινὰ περιοδευθῆναι (v) Ὑπεδέξατο
en: Περιοδευθῆναι. Why should I explain a word that is not obscure? Why then a Note? So that the epistle of St Nilus, no. 285, book 2, may be emended: 'Ἵνα γνῷς ... δοῦλον', that is, 'that you may know most clearly both the adversary's rage and Christ's solicitude, who cared for you as a most beloved servant, and as quickly as possible'. Περιοδυνήσαντος (having caused pain) gives a plainly contrary sense.

text: Σιανθείς. Verbum minus usitatum Dorothei, doctrina 71: Εἶδον πολλοὺς τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑβρίζοντας καὶ σιαίνοντας αὐτόν. Aspiciebam multos fratres contumelia afficientes et commoventes seu irritantes ipsum.
anchorLine: ταῦτα παρ' αὐτῆς καὶ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα, σιανθεῖς (x)
en: Σιανθείς. A rather unusual word of Dorotheus, teaching 71: 'I saw many of the brothers insulting and vexing him.' (Latin: I saw many brothers treating him with insult and stirring or provoking him.)

text: Καμάτους. In Auctario novissimo Combefisii, t. I, p. 199 B. Irenæus, Ὁ ὄνος τύπον εἶχε σώματος Χριστοῦ· ἐφ' ὃν πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐκ καμάτων ἀναπαυόμενοι, ὡς ὑπ' ὀχήματος βαστάζονται. Vix quemquam dubitaturum arbitror, quin legi debeat καμάτων. Asina Balaami, figura erat corporis Christi; super quem cuncti homines a laboribus quiescentes, velut curru gestantur.
anchorLine: ἡδονὴν ἀπολέσαι τοὺς τοιούτους καμάτους (y) ὅσους
en: Καμάτους (labors). In Combefis's latest Auctarium, vol. 1, p. 199 B. Irenaeus: 'The ass was a type of the body of Christ, on which all people, resting from their labors, are carried as in a vehicle.' I think hardly anyone will doubt that one should read καμάτων. Balaam's ass was a figure of Christ's body, on which all men, resting from their labors, are carried as in a carriage.

text: Πλεονεκτεῖ. Accipitur πλεονεκτεῖν in bonam et in malam partem: in bonam, apud Cyrillum, in Nahum, p. 477 E: Ὤοντο γὰρ ὅτι νενικήκασι οὐκ ἑκόντος αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὁμοῦ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐπαμύνουσαν αὐτοῖς πεπλεονεκτήκασι χεῖρα. In malam, apud eumdem, ad Michæam, p. 452 D: Ἐπονηρεύσαντο, πεπλεονεκτήκασιν (sic malo quam πεπλεονάκασιν) καὶ διωγμοὺς εἰργάσαντο κατὰ τῶν ἁγίων.
anchorLine: Εἶπεν πάλιν ὁ γέρων· Πλεονεκτεῖ (z) ὁ ταπεινὸς
en: Πλεονεκτεῖ. The verb πλεονεκτεῖν is taken both in a good and in a bad sense. In a good sense, in Cyril on Nahum, p. 477 E: 'for they thought they had conquered not with his consent, and together with the Jews they have gained the advantage over the hand that defended them.' In a bad sense, in the same on Micah, p. 452 D: 'They acted wickedly, they have overreached (so I prefer this to πεπλεονάκασιν) and carried out persecutions against the saints.'

text: Ἱκανήν. Tollo per levem occasionem leve mendum ab Aristea De LXX, quæst. 17: Μὴ πολλῶν ὀρέγου, τῶν δ' ἱκανῶν πρὸς τὸ βασιλεύειν. Interpr. Neque multas jurisdictiones ad tuum regnum pertrahere cupias; scribendo τῶν δὲ ἱκανῶν. Hoc est: Ne multa cupias, sed quæ sufficiunt ad regnandum.
anchorLine: νὴν (a) ὥραν, ἕως οὗ συστείλαι καὶ ἐκ τοῦ μέσου τὰ
en: Ἱκανήν. I remove, on a slight pretext, a slight error, taken from Aristeas, On the LXX, question 17: 'Do not strive after many things, but those sufficient for reigning.' The translator: 'Do not desire to draw many jurisdictions into your kingdom', by writing τῶν δὲ ἱκανῶν. That is: do not desire many things, but what suffices for ruling.

text: Καθαρά. Ex sensu verti bellaria. Neque enim alibi ejusmodi significatione inveni. At interpres Ambrosius quod non intelligebat, laxius transtulit. In Glossariis, καθαρὸς ἄρτος, Siliginenm. Quid vero sit cœna pura neminem latere potest.
anchorLine: μοι ὀλίγα ὠά, καὶ ὀλίγα καθαρά (b). Λέγω αὐτῷ·
en: Καθαρά. I translated it by sense as 'bellaria' (sweetmeats). For I have not found the word in such a meaning elsewhere. The translator Ambrosius, because he did not understand it, rendered it loosely. In the Glossaries, καθαρὸς ἄρτος is 'Siliginenm' (wheaten bread). What a pure supper is, no one can fail to know.

text: Φώτισμα. Quemadmodum Ecclesia vocatur locus in quo fit cœtus, ἐκκλησία, ita hoc capite et sequenti φώτισμα dicitur locus in quo illuminatio, φώτισμα, baptismus, celebratur: qui locus vulgo nominatur φωτιστήριον, φωτιστήρ, βαπτιστήριον, βαπτιστήρ, baptisterium. An vero apud alium scriptorem φώτισμα hoc sensu accipiatur, plane nescio. Non tamen multum dissimiliter in Symmictis Allatii, p. I, p. 36 et 62, locus est βάπτισις, et βάπτισις Χριστοῦ. Quod vero spectat ad φώτισμα seu φωτισμὸν, baptismum, observavi Theodorum Gazam interpretem Orationum sancti Chrysostomi de incomprehensibili Dei natura, orat. 4, p. 775 A, t. I, posuisse post sacri lavacri splendorem, pro eo quod Græce est, μετὰ τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν τοῦ λουτροῦ. Quia nimirum legebat, ἀπόφαυσιν, nomine minus usitato. Quemadmodum διαφαύματος scripserat auctor Martyrii SS. Maximi, Dudæ et Quintiliani, n. 3. (Qua voce etiam utitur Cyrillus Scythopolita in Vita Sabæ, cap. 17 et 67.) Ediderunt autem, διαφαίματος, et tentaverunt corrigere, διαυγάσματος. Ad Aprilis 13, Pseudochrysostomus, De turture, seu De Ecclesia: Εἴ τις ἐστιν ἐνταῦθα κατηχούμενος, μετανοείτω, προσερχέσθω τῷ Θεῷ, τῷ ὕδατι βαπτιζέσθω, τῷ βλέμματι (an πνεύματι) φωτιζέσθω.
anchorLine: λεως Κοιανέων, ἐν ᾗ ἐστιν φώτισμα (c), ἐν τοῖς
en: Φώτισμα. As the place where an assembly takes place is called Ecclesia (ἐκκλησία), so in this chapter and the next φώτισμα is the name of the place where illumination (φώτισμα), that is baptism, is celebrated; the place commonly called φωτιστήριον, φωτιστήρ, βαπτιστήριον, βαπτιστήρ, baptisterium. Whether φώτισμα is taken in this sense in another writer, I do not know at all. Yet something not very different is found in Allatius's Symmicta, part 1, pp. 36 and 62: the place is 'baptism', and 'baptism of Christ'. As to φώτισμα or φωτισμός, baptism, I have noted that Theodorus Gaza, translator of the Orations of St Chrysostom On the Incomprehensible Nature of God, oration 4, p. 775 A, vol. 1, put 'after the splendor of the sacred bath' for the Greek 'after the enjoyment of the bath', since he evidently read ἀπόφαυσιν, a less common noun. As the author of the Martyrdom of SS Maximus, Dada and Quintilian, no. 3, had written διαφαύματος (the same word is also used by Cyril of Scythopolis in the Life of Sabas, chs. 17 and 67). They have printed διαφαίματος and tried to correct to διαυγάσματος. On 13 April, Pseudo-Chrysostom, On the Turtle-dove, or On the Church: 'If anyone here is a catechumen, let him repent, come to God, be baptized with water, be illumined by the sight (or perhaps by the Spirit).'

text: Nudam eam sancto oleo inungere.] Obtinuit olim tam viros quam feminas nudas corporibus baptizare, itaque inungere.
en: In the past it was customary to baptize both men and women naked in body, and therefore to anoint them.

text: Saracenos.] De monachis a Saracenis interfectis Martyrologium Romanum 19 Februarii: « In Palæstina commemoratio sanctorum monachorum, et aliorum martyrum, qui a Sarracenis sub duce Alamundaro ob fidem Christi sævissime cæsi sunt. » Ubi Baronius notat: Iisdem cæsi sunt hi Sarracenorum incursionibus, quarum mentio habetur in rebus gestis sancti Joannis Silentiarii, quas refert Metaphrastes die 13 Maii, itemque in Vita sancti Sabæ abbatis apud eumdem die 5 Decembris, ac in Actis et in sancti Euthymii abbatis, quæ idem recitat die 20 Januarii. Consentiunt iisdem quæ habentur in Prato spirituali, cap. 21 et ?9. Una eademque persecutio Sarracenorum sanctos monachos diversisque diebus occidit, ut non mireris si inferius de monachis cæsis a Sarracenis sæpe agatur. Hactenus Baronius.
en: On the monks killed by the Saracens, the Roman Martyrology for 19 February: 'In Palestine, commemoration of the holy monks and other martyrs who were most cruelly slain by the Saracens under their leader Alamundarus for the faith of Christ.' Baronius notes there: these were killed in the same Saracen raids mentioned in the acts of St John the Silentiary (which Metaphrastes gives on 13 May), likewise in the Life of St Sabas the abbot (same author, 5 December), and in the Acts of St Euthymius the abbot (same author, 20 January). What is found in the Spiritual Meadow, chapters 21 and ?9, agrees with these. One and the same Saracen persecution killed holy monks on different days, so you need not wonder that later there is frequent talk of monks killed by Saracens. So far Baronius.

text: Ex scholaribus.] In Græco est, ἀπὸ Σχολαρίων. Hervetus verterat scholasticus. Ex militiæ ordine scholares sunt.
en: In the Greek it is 'from the Scholarii'. Hervetus had translated 'scholasticus'. The 'scholares' belong to the order of the army.

text: Verba sanctæ oblationis.] Infra, cap. 196, habes item verba oblationis a puero prolata, et panem una cum saxo, quod pro altari erat, igne cœlesti consumptum; quod reverentiæ causa factum credo, ne videlicet tam sanctum mysterium puerilibus ludicris exponeretur.
en: Below, ch. 196, you have likewise the words of the oblation spoken by a boy, and the bread together with the stone that served as an altar consumed by heavenly fire; I believe this was done out of reverence, lest so holy a mystery be exposed to children's games.

text: Babylæ.] Ut hic ecclesiam ingrediens, audita fortuita Evangelii sententia ad meliorem frugem convertitur, idem pluribus aliis contigit. Vide dicta ad Vitam sancti Antonii cap. 2, n. 9.
en: As here someone entering a church, hearing a chance saying of the Gospel, is turned to a better life, the same happened to many others. See what is said on the Life of St Anthony, ch. 2, no. 9.

text: Eliæ.] De Elia in exsilium misso exstat mentio in Vita sancti Sabæ, auctore Cyrillo, 5 Decemb. Vide Baronium, tomo VI, anno Christi 513, Symmachi papæ 15, Anastasii imp. 23, et Theodorici regis 21. Quod vero hic habetur, post duos dies, monet Baronius tomo eodem, anno Christi 518, Hormisdæ papæ 5, Anastasii imp. 28, Theodorici regis 26, duos, inquiens, nimirum dies a scriptis litteris, non autem ab obitu Anastasii numerandos. Certe in Vita sancti Sabæ a Cyrillo monacho conscripta, 5 Decembris, Elias ipse ex visione et revelatione narrat se decimo die Anastasium ea hora mortuum secuturum.
en: Of Elias sent into exile there is mention in the Life of St Sabas by Cyril, 5 December. See Baronius, vol. 6, year of Christ 513, Symmachus pope 15, Anastasius emperor 23, Theodoric king 21. As for what is read here, 'after two days', Baronius warns, same volume, year 518, that the two days are to be counted from the writing of the letters and not from Anastasius's death. Certainly in the Life of St Sabas written by Cyril, 5 December, Elias himself says from a vision and revelation that he would follow Anastasius in death on the tenth day, at that hour.

text: Accendamus ignem.] Frequens ea in causa fidei ad ignem provocatio. Exempla aliquot congessi in dissertat. de Fide hæreticis servanda cap. 12.
en: Appeal to fire was frequent in matters of faith. I have collected some examples in my dissertation on keeping faith with heretics, ch. 12.

text: Anastasii.] Baronius, tomo VI, anno Christi 495, Gelasii papæ 4, Anastasii imp. 5, Theodorici regis 3, agit de Euphemio in exsilium misso ab Anastasio; anno vero Christi 511, Symmachi papæ 13, Anastasii imp. 21, Theodorici regis 19, de Macedonio in exsilium ab eodem Anastasio pulso. Quæ hic habes de quatuordecim deletis, intellige de annis. Zonaras, tomo III, in Anastasio: Καὶ αὖθις ὄναρ ἰδεῖν λέγεται ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐκεῖνος, ἄνδρα τινὰ φοβερὸν, τόμον κατέχοντα, καὶ λέγοντα πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἰδοὺ διὰ τὴν κακοπιστίαν σου, ἀπαλείφω τῆς ζωῆς σου ἔτη τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα: « Denuo aliud vidisse somnium memoratur rex, virum terribilem, qui librum manu gestaret et diceret: Ecce ob perversitatem fidei tuæ, annos XIV vitæ duæ deleo. » Vide Baronium, tomo VI, anno Christi 518, Hormisdæ papæ 5, Anastasii imperatoris 28, Theodorici regis 26.
en: Baronius, vol. 6, year of Christ 495, treats of Euphemius sent into exile by Anastasius; and in 511, of Macedonius driven into exile by the same Anastasius. What you have here about the 'fourteen deleted', understand as years. Zonaras, vol. 3, under Anastasius: 'And again that emperor is said to have seen in a dream a fearsome man holding a scroll and saying to him: Behold, because of your bad faith I blot out fourteen years of your life.' (Latin: Again the king is said to have seen another dream, a terrible man holding a book in his hand and saying: Behold, because of the perversity of your faith I delete fourteen years of your life.) See Baronius, vol. 6, year 518, Hormisdas pope 5, Anastasius emperor 28, Theodoric king 26.

text: Minutorum viginti.] Existimo in Græco fuisse λεπτῶν vel φόλεων, nam deest hic nobis ille textus. Infra, cap. 134: « Accipiebatque quotidianum stipendium novem minuta. »
en: I think the Greek had λεπτῶν or φόλεων, for that text is missing here. Below, ch. 134: 'And he received a daily wage of nine minuta.'

text: Et de adoratione.] Septima synodus generalis, quæ est secunda Nicæna, actione 4 et 5 exemplum hoc ex hoc libro Græce citat.
en: The seventh general synod, which is the second Nicene, in its 4th and 5th sessions cites this example from this book in Greek.

text: Lictores qui assistebant.] Græce φραγγελιβαί. Intelligit lictores ducis. Hervetus verterat, et cæteri qui assistebant.
en: In Greek 'φραγγελιβαί'. It means the duke's lictors (attendants). Hervetus had translated 'and the others who were standing by'.

text: Ut canonarchæ.] Hoc Herveto deerat. Appositum ex Græco, in quo κανόναρχος, id est, qui canoni psalmorum cantandorum præest.
en: Hervetus lacked this. It is added from the Greek, which has κανόναρχος, that is, one who presides over the canon of psalms to be sung.

text: Senum gesta.] In Græco est βιβλίον Γεροντικόν. Ita liber ille appellabatur. Ex Gerontico ms. quædam vertit Raderus noster parte III Viridarii sui. Sic Verba Seniorum dicebantur quæ Patres illi scite proferebant.
en: The Greek has 'Gerontikon book'; that book was so called. Our Raderus translated some things from a manuscript Gerontikon in part 3 of his Viridarium. 'Sayings of the Elders' was likewise the name of what those Fathers wisely uttered.

text: Mittite thymiama in thuribulum.] Jam olim in honorem sanctorum thymiama incendi solitum.
en: Already of old incense was customarily burned in honor of the saints.

text: Thalelæi.] Raderus noster, Viridarii parte I, putat hunc eumdem cum Thalelæo martyre tempore Numeriani, de quo Menæa, 20 Maii. Sed vereor ut ratio temporis aliud suadeat: siquidem Moschus audivit ex Petro, quæ de hoc hic habentur; at Petrus centenis annis a Numeriani imperio distat. Aliter
en: Our Raderus, in part 1 of the Viridarium, thinks this man the same as the martyr Thalelaeus in the time of Numerian, of whom the Menaea, 20 May. But I fear the chronology suggests otherwise: Moschus heard from Peter what is told here about him, and Peter is a hundred years distant from Numerian's rule. Otherwise ... (the note breaks off at the foot of the page with 'Aliter').
unreadable: note breaks off after 'Aliter' at the foot of the page; continues on p-0171

text: (continuation) opinandi occasio forte fuit, quod hic dicatur Cilix; et alter in Menæis dicatur Azarbi in Cilicia abditus. Sed ibidem dicitur profectus a Libano; quare Libanites est. Verisimilius hunc eumdem esse cum Thalelæo Theodoreti, cap. 28 Philothei, quia uterque Cilix, et idem de pœnitentia dictum habent. Theodoretus eum vidit, et Moschus audivit narrari ex Petro. Sic tempora convenire potuerunt.
en: (Continued from p-0170) ...the occasion for the opinion was perhaps that this man is called a Cilician, and the other in the Menaea is said to be (Azarbi) hidden in Cilicia. But there he is said to have set out from Lebanon, so he is a Lebanese. It is more likely that he is the same as Theodoret's Thalelaeus (Philotheus, ch. 28), since both are Cilicians and have the same thing said about repentance. Theodoret saw him, and Moschus heard it told by Peter. In this way the dates could agree.
unreadable: one letter of 'Azarbi' ambiguous (b/h); this block is the continuation at the top of the page, preceded by 'Aliter' at the foot of p-0170

text: Per Serapim facite.] Ita locus hic nunc restitutus ex Græco. Ante nullo sensu erat, Serapim facite.
en: This place is now restored from the Greek in this way. Before, it made no sense: 'Serapim facite'.

text: Carabum.] Ex sequentibus intelligitur quid carabus sit. Dicitur enim: Produc scapham.
en: From what follows one understands what a 'carabus' is. For it is said: 'Bring out the boat.'

text: Tetrapylum.] Porticus vel templum quatuor columnarum ordinibus constans. In Græco omittitur, ad Orientem juxta Tetrapylum; ejus loco est, τὴν ἐπονομαζομένην τῆς Δωροθέας: quæ cognominabatur Dorotheæ, de beatæ Virginis æde. Tetrapyli Alexandrini meminit Sophronius archiepiscopus Hierosolymitanus, agens de miraculis Joannis et Cyri martyrum: Εἴσελθε γοῦν εἰς Ἀλεξάνδρειαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ Τετραπύλῳ νήστης καθεύδησον: « Ingredere itaque Alexandriam, et in magno Tetrapylo jejunus dormi. » Quæ citantur in septima synodo, act. 4.
en: Tetrapylum: a portico or temple consisting of four rows of columns. In the Greek 'to the east beside the Tetrapylum' is omitted; in its place is 'the one called of Dorothea', i.e. which was surnamed Dorothea's, of the church of the Blessed Virgin. Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, mentions the Alexandrian Tetrapylum in his account of the miracles of John and Cyrus the martyrs: 'Go into Alexandria, and in the great Tetrapylum sleep fasting.' These words are cited in the seventh synod, session 4.

text: Epitimia.] Retinui Græcam vocem ἐπιτίμια, id est, multas. Ecclesiastici quidam scriptores Latini hoc usurpant vocabulum. Vide Onomasticon.
en: I kept the Greek word epitimia, that is, penalties. Some Latin ecclesiastical writers use this word. See the Onomasticon.

text: Quibus manibus.] Manibus olim viri, feminæ linteolo Eucharistiam excipiebant et sumebant.
en: In the past men received and took the Eucharist in their hands; women with a linen cloth.

text: Apocrisiarii.] Infra, cap. 145, misso quodam apocrisiario suo. Est fere apocrisiarius, Græcis ἀποκρισιάριος, legatus ecclesiæ negotia tractans.
en: Below, ch. 145: 'having sent a certain apocrisiarius of his'. An apocrisiarius, in Greek ἀποκρισιάριος, is roughly an envoy handling the affairs of a church.

text: Templum sancti Quirici.] Videndum an non hic ipse, qui sanctus Quiriacus in Romano Martyrologio dicitur, 29 Septembris: « In Palæstina sancti Quiriaci anachoretæ, » cujus Vitam a Metaphraste descriptam apud Laurentium Surium eo mense habes.
en: It should be considered whether this is not the same man who is called St Quiriacus in the Roman Martyrology, 29 September: 'In Palestine, of St Quiriacus the anchorite', whose Life written by Metaphrastes you have in Laurentius Surius under that month.

text: Sarraceni.] Vide hic dicta supra, ad cap. 21, de Sarracenorum incursionibus, et martyribus sub iis passis.
en: See what is said above, at ch. 21, about the Saracen raids and the martyrs who suffered under them.

text: Responsum.] Quid hic responsum sit, jure hæreas. Suspicor in Græco fuisse προσφωνάριον, quod interpres prima et obvia notione responsum vertit. Videndum tamen num hic vertendum sit, sportam, vel simile quid. Suggerebat videlicet monacho cogitatio, ut non adoraret crucem, sed in cellam rediret, et sportas texeret. Vide dicta sup., ad lib. v, libel. x, n. 18. Quod si responsum hic communi notione intelligitur, cape fratrem hunc missum pro responsis cœnobii. Sic infra, cap. 235: « aliquis manens in cœnobio missus est pro responsis cœnobii. »
en: You may rightly hesitate over what 'responsum' is here. I suspect the Greek had a word (garbled in the print, something like προσφωνάριον), which the translator rendered 'responsum' by its first and obvious meaning. It should be considered whether it ought rather to be translated 'sporta' (basket) or something similar: the thought suggested to the monk that he not worship the cross but return to his cell and weave baskets. See what is said above on book 5, booklet 10, no. 18. But if 'responsum' is taken in its ordinary sense, understand this brother as sent for the replies of the monastery. So below, ch. 235: 'someone living in a monastery was sent for the monastery's replies.'
unreadable: Greek word printed with damaged letters (read προσφωνάριον by shape, uncertain); chapter number 235 has a damaged middle digit

text: Cantheliam.] Sunt canthelia, κανθήλια, onera asinis imponi solita.
en: 'Canthelia' (κανθήλια) are loads usually placed on asses.

text: Sibino.] Idem mox accurrit caput 123: « vestitum colobio de sibino. » Quid sibinum sit, nondum mihi lectum.
en: The same word soon occurs in chapter 123: 'clothed in a colobium of sibinum'. What sibinum is, I have not yet read.

text: Burdones.] Vide dicta ad Vitam Simeonis Stylitæ, cap. 20, n. 24.
en: See what is said on the Life of Simeon Stylites, ch. 20, no. 24.

text: In sancta Christi Dei nostri resurrectione.] Hoc loco Resurrectio est templum Christi resurrectioni dicatum.
en: In this place 'Resurrection' is the temple dedicated to Christ's resurrection.

text: Syncello seu assessori suo.] Servavi Græcum vocabulum syncellus, qui apud Græcos est proximus a patriarcha.
en: I kept the Greek word 'syncellus', who among the Greeks is next to the patriarch.

text: In membranis valde pulchrum.] Græce est: ἐν σώματι πολὺ καλῷ.
en: The Greek is: 'in a very fair body'.

text: Zachariæ.] Zachariam non perfecte credidisse angelo, Lucas, cap. 1, testatur. Non dubitavit Zacharias de Dei potentia, qui noverat Isaacum de sterili Sara et Abrahamo genitum, sed de voluntate Dei. Quare in supplicium dubitationis cessit illi taciturnitas. Augustinus lib. L Homiliarum, homil. 44: « Accepit Zacharias supplicium taciturnitatis, merito infidelitatis: quia non credidit, tacuit; sic enim recte dictum est psalmo cxv: Credidi, propter quod locutus sum; quia Zacharias non credebat, merito non loquebatur. » Ambrosius, lib. II in Lucam: « Incredulitas Zachariæ affatum eripuerat et auditum. »
en: Luke, ch. 1, testifies that Zacharias did not fully believe the angel. Zacharias did not doubt God's power, he who knew that Isaac was born of barren Sarah and Abraham, but doubted God's will. Hence silence became the punishment of his doubt. Augustine, book 50 of the Homilies, homily 44: 'Zacharias received the punishment of silence, deservedly for unbelief: because he did not believe, he was silent; for it is rightly said in Psalm 115: I believed, therefore have I spoken; because Zacharias did not believe, he deservedly did not speak.' Ambrose, book 2 on Luke: 'The unbelief of Zacharias had taken away his speech and hearing.'

text: Leone.] Baronius, tomo VI, anno Christi 449, Leonis papæ 10, Theodosii 42, Valentiniani 25, impp., ad hanc de Leonis encyclica (quæ inter epistolas Leonis est 10) visionem notat: Sed præstat, inquit, audire potius sententiam Petri, quam visionem Petri, dicentis: Firmiorem quavis visione habemus sermonem propheticum (II Pet. I), etc. Etenim majorem sibi ea epistola fidem vindicat ex divinis Scripturis, traditionibusque sanctæ Ecclesiæ, et communi sanctorum Patrum consensu, quam ex recensita modo visione. Hactenus Baronius. Qui ad sequentis capitis visionem de sancto Eulogio defensore epistolæ sancti Leonis ista quoque addit: At certioris fidei certiorisque quoque testimonii apud me est de epistola sancti Leonis publica concilii œcumenici Chalcedonensis assertio et prædicatio, quam quælibet privatæ hujusmodi visiones. Ita Baronius. Vide apud eumdem plura de hac Leonis encyclica elogia. Ad sequens caput 149, de Leone ita notat Baronius anno 461, Hilarii papæ 1, Leonis 5, et Severi 1, impp. Sed quid est: Omnia tibi sunt dimissa peccata, præter manuum impositionem? Num peccata ex parte dimitti possunt? Minime gentium, si ad culpam referas. Cæterum quoad pœnam dici debent dimissa fuisse sancto Leoni peccata. Quod enim facile sit in his peccare etiam prudentem episcopum, jure sanctus Apostolus monet ita Timotheum: Nemini cito manus imposueris, neque communicaveris peccatis alienis (I Tim. V). Illis ergo remanebat sanctus Leo delictorum pœnis obligatus, quæ illi perpetrassent, qui ab eo indigne promoti fuissent ad ordines. Tunc namque dicuntur præsules communicare peccatis alienis, dum indignis conferunt honores et ministeria. Hinc sibi timens Propheta rex, ait: Ab alienis parce servo tuo (Psal. XVIII). Quod si hæc fiunt in viridi, quid fiet in arido (Luc. XXIII)? Leone quis sanctior atque prudentior, ut tantum periculum liber transiliat?
en: Baronius, vol. 6, year of Christ 449, Leo pope 10, emperors Theodosius 42 and Valentinian 25, notes on this vision about Leo's encyclical (which is letter 10 among Leo's letters): 'But it is better, he says, to hear Peter's judgment rather than Peter's vision, when he says: We have a more sure prophetic word than any vision (2 Pet. 1), etc. For that letter claims greater credit for itself from the divine Scriptures, from the traditions of holy Church and the common consent of the holy Fathers than from the vision just recounted.' So far Baronius. He adds on the vision in the following chapter concerning St Eulogius, defender of St Leo's letter: 'But of surer faith and surer testimony in my view is the public assertion and proclamation of the ecumenical council of Chalcedon about St Leo's letter than any private visions of this kind.' So Baronius; see more in him on this encyclical eulogy of Leo. On the next chapter, 149, Baronius notes about Leo in the year 461, Hilary pope 1, Leo 5, Severus 1, emperors: 'But what is this: All your sins are forgiven, except the laying on of hands? Can sins be forgiven in part? By no means, if you refer it to guilt. But as regards punishment, the sins can be said to have been remitted to St Leo. For that even a prudent bishop may easily sin in these matters, the holy Apostle rightly warns Timothy: Lay hands hastily on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins (1 Tim. 5). So St Leo remained liable to the penalties of the offenses committed by those whom he had unworthily promoted to orders. For then prelates are said to share in others' sins when they confer honors and ministries on the unworthy. Hence the prophet-king, fearing for himself, says: Spare thy servant from the sins of others (Ps. 18). But if these things happen in the green wood, what will happen in the dry (Luke 23)? Who is holier and wiser than Leo, to leap clear of so great a danger?'

text: Flabellum.] Græco ῥιπίδιον. Ejus in sacro faciendo usus, quod diaconus gestat.
en: In Greek ῥιπίδιον. It is used in performing the sacred rite, and the deacon carries it.

text: Conopionem.] Servavit interpres Græcam inflexionem, quod nunc κωνωπεῖον, nunc κωνωπεών dicitur, conopeum Latinis usitatum, pro textili tentorio culicibus arcendis comparato.
en: The translator kept the Greek inflection, which is called now κωνωπεῖον, now κωνωπεών; Latin writers use 'conopeum', for a woven tent made to keep off gnats.

text: Membranas.] Ut hic membranas ad aquam pluviam excipiendam explicant, sic alii nautæ vellera et pelles exponunt, tum ad pluviam tum ad rorem colligendum.
en: As here they spread out skins to catch rainwater, so other sailors put out fleeces and hides, either to collect rain or dew.

text: Arena.] Nec arena littoralis, nec quocunque modo madefacta potest esse materia baptismi; siquidem materia baptismi aqua esse debet, qua quis ablui possit. Vide Scholasticos in III partem divi Thomæ, et in primis Franciscum nostrum Suarez, t. III, in III partem, ad q. 66, art. 4, disp. 20, sect. 1.
en: Neither beach sand nor sand wetted in any way can be the matter of baptism; since the matter of baptism must be water, by which one can be washed. See the Scholastics on the third part of St Thomas, and especially our Francisco Suárez, vol. 3, on the third part, q. 66, art. 4, disp. 20, sect. 1.

text: Infusa.] Quæ hæc infusa sint, difficile divinare. Nam varii cibi infundi possunt et macerari. Hic ante: « paucisque infusis cibariis. » Aliquoties in Theodoreto supra habens « lentem aqua madefactam. » Hic infra, cap. 184: « Infundebat et paximatia seu madefaciebat. »
en: What these 'infusa' are is hard to guess, for various foods can be soaked and softened. Earlier here: 'and a few soaked foods'. Several times above in Theodoret, 'lentils soaked in water'. Here below, ch. 184: 'He soaked or moistened the biscuits.'

text: Joannis.] Citatur hæc historia in septima synodo generali, quæ est II Nicæna, act. 5, ubi pro Saraphas habetur Araphas.
en: This story is cited in the seventh general synod, the second Nicene, session 5, where 'Araphas' stands in place of 'Saraphas'.

text: Spetlum.] Reposui hoc ex Græco textu σπέ-τλον, quod interpres omiserat, videtur fenestra intelligi ex speculari lapide.
en: Spetlum. I have put this back from the Greek text (σπέτλον as printed, broken across the line), which the translator had omitted; it seems a window of transparent stone (selenite) is meant.
unreadable: Greek word printed broken (σπέ-/τλον), possibly misprint for σπήλιον/σπέλεον; transcribed as printed

text: Miliarisia.] Retinui Græcani vocem μιλια-
en: I kept the Greek word μιλια... (the note breaks off at the foot of the page; continues on p-0172).
unreadable: note cut off mid-word at the foot; continues on p-0172

text: (continuation) ρίσια, quod certi nummi genus. Interpres numismata verterat.
en: (Continued from p-0171, Miliarisia) ...ρίσια, a certain kind of coin. The translator had rendered it 'numismata' (coins).
unreadable: first letters of the Greek word sit at the page edge/cut off; continuation of note 40 begun at foot of p-0171

text: Apparentiam.] Græce est, φαντιτίαν, id est, cupiditas se ostentandi.
en: In Greek it is (φαντασίαν as printed 'φαντιτίαν'), that is, desire to show oneself off.
unreadable: Greek word printed with damaged letters (φαντητίαν/φαντασίαν); transcribed as seen

text: Chrysostomus.] Henricus Savilius, notis suis ad tomum VIII Chrysostomi Græce a se editi, existimat non indignum observatu temporibus inter quintam synodum, anno 553, et sextam, anno 680 celebratam (quibus Georgium Vitæ Chrysostomi scriptorem vixisse probabile esse ait) Chrysostomi cognomen ignotum fuisse. Sed refellit eum Joannes Moschus seu Sophronius hic, qui tempore Georgii istius vixere, et hujus cognominis Chrysostomi meminere.
en: Henry Savile, in his notes on vol. 8 of Chrysostom (edited by him in Greek), thinks it worth observing that in the period between the fifth synod (553) and the sixth (680), in which he says George, the writer of Chrysostom's Life, probably lived, the surname Chrysostom was unknown. But John Moschus or Sophronius here refutes him: they lived in that George's time and mention this surname of Chrysostom.

text: Gregorii.] Habetur hæc narratio in Vita sancti Gregorii, lib. II, cap. 45 per Joannem Diaconum scripta, qui eam citat ex libro, qui a Græcis Λειμών dicitur, a Latinis vero intelligitur Campus vel Pratum. Qui hic ipse liber est, quem præ manibus habemus. Citat ille ex interpretatione præceptoris sui, ubi quod hic est, tunicam non habeo, vertit ille, casulam non habeo. Eodem modo idem, lib. IV, c. 63: « Et jussit mihi dari casulam, et necessitates meas omnes. » Ubi noster interpres Ambr. Camaldulensis hic, cap. 181: « Jubens mihi dari quæcunque erant necessaria, » decurtate. Omisit enim illud de casula seu tunica.
en: This story is in the Life of St Gregory, book 2, ch. 45, written by John the Deacon, who cites it from the book called Leimon by the Greeks, which the Latins understand as Campus or Pratum (Meadow). This is the very book we have in hand. He cites it from the translation of his teacher, where our text's 'I have no tunic' he renders 'I have no chasuble'. In the same way, book 4, ch. 63: 'And he ordered a chasuble given to me, and all my needs.' Where our translator Ambrose of Camaldoli here, ch. 181, has 'ordering all necessities to be given to me', abridged; for he omitted the part about the chasuble or tunic.

text: Nomicum seu dispensatorem.] Varia Nomici, Νομικοῦ, ut hic in Græco textu, est significatio. Hic dispensatorem significat.
en: 'Nomicus' (Νομικοῦ), as here in the Greek text, has various meanings. Here it means a steward or dispenser.

text: A notario perfecte, et a grammatico sufficienter.] Notarius hic est qui præest pueris ad prima elementa et litteras formandas. Vide Onomasticon.
en: Here the 'notarius' is the one who presides over boys for the first elements and for forming letters. See the Onomasticon.

text: Idcirco sunt baptizati.] Baronius, tomo III, anno Christi 310, § 13. Significat nimirum ejusmodi sacramentum consecutos, non autem, quod aiunt, rem sacramenti, ipsam gratiam abluentem peccata.
en: Baronius, vol. 3, year of Christ 310, section 13. It means that they obtained the sacrament as such, but not, as they say, the thing of the sacrament, the very grace washing away sins.

text: Mulier.] Joannes Cassianus, collat. XVIII, cap. 14, simile exemplum religiosæ feminæ, quæ patientiæ acquirendæ intenta erat, narrat.
en: John Cassian, Conference 18, ch. 14, tells a similar example of a devout woman who was intent on acquiring patience.

text: Sophistam Sophronium appellat Jo. Moschus, cap. 92, et in Præfat. [V. inf. vol. IX, p. 22 et vet.]
anchorLine: Sophronius, Damascenus, Joannis Moschi familiaris, ex sophista (a) monachus S. Sabæ
en: John Moschus calls Sophronius 'the sophist', ch. 92 and in the Preface. [See below, vol. 9, p. 22 of the old (edition).]
unreadable: end of the note read from the left half; last words after 'p. 22' ('et vet.' / 'e vet.') partly cut by the column; transcribed as best read

text: Alii 636, quorum sententiam Papebrochius loco laudato oppugnat probabilibus argumentis. FABR. Saxius in Onom. lit. II, pag. 75, prodit, Sophronium ab a. 633 fuisse patriarcham Hierosolymitanum, laudatque Pagii Critic. Baron. 633, VI, VII, p. 274-276, a. 636 (quo Sophronius e vita decessit), III, IV, p. 314. 315, tom. IX, atque in Analectis Moshemii, Hist. ecclesiast. sæc. VII, part. II, cap. 2, § 5. (0) — Caveus, in Hist. litterar. script. eccl. I, p. 579, ad a. 629. Hoc demum anno, n. 629, Sophronium scribit, patriarchæ Hierosolymitani dignitatem esse consecutum, et, indefessus, ait, orthodoxæ veritatis vindex, qui præsens Alexandriæ factus a. 633, Cyrum sub obtentu pacis ineundæ hæresin in Ecclesiam invexisse strenue exclamavit, et communionem ei renuntiavit, etc. Tum recenset ejus scripta. Add. Lambec. Comm. de Cæsar. III, p. 137 seq. not. 2, ubi is de Sophronio ejusque ætate agit, aliosque laudat VV. DD. de illo disputantes, et supra, vol. VIII, p. 353, not. q. HARL.
anchorLine: ad 638 (b) patriarcha Hierosolymitanus
en: Others say 636; Papebroch, in the place cited, attacks their opinion with probable arguments. Fabricius: Saxius, in the Onomasticon, part 2, p. 75, reports that Sophronius was patriarch of Jerusalem from 633, and cites Pagi's Critica on Baronius, 633, vol. 6, 7, pp. 274-276, year 636 (when Sophronius died), 3, 4, pp. 314-315, vol. 9, and in Mosheim's Analecta, Ecclesiastical History, 7th century, part 2, ch. 2, section 5. Cave, in his History of ecclesiastical writers, vol. 1, p. 579, at the year 629, writes that only in this year Sophronius attained the dignity of patriarch of Jerusalem, and, tireless defender of orthodox truth, being present in Alexandria in 633, he cried out vigorously that Cyrus, under pretext of making peace, had brought heresy into the Church, and renounced communion with him, etc. Then he reviews his writings. Add Lambeck, Commentary on Caesar, vol. 3, p. 137 ff., note 2, where he treats of Sophronius and his age and cites other learned men who discuss him, and above, vol. 8, p. 353, note q. Harles.
unreadable: bracketed '(0)' in the text is printed so; possibly '(c)' or '(1)'

text: Vid. supra, vol. VII, p. 455. HARL.
anchorLine: Pseudo-Dorothei, Tyrii, (c) quem cum
en: See above, vol. 7, p. 455. Harles.

text: Cod. 59, n. 13, pag. 264 seq. ed. Kollar. — Paris. in bibl. publ. cod. 186, n. 2, excerpta ex illo encomio. HARL.
anchorLine: Aliud apud Lambecium, III, pag. 100 (d).

text: Hallucinatur Harlesius; etenim sive in volumine septimo, ubi Patrum sermones de Præcursore, sive etiam in aliis Combefisii tomis, hunc frustra quæres. EDIT.
en: Harles is mistaken; for whether in the seventh volume, where the Fathers' sermons on the Forerunner are, or even in other volumes of Combefis, you will look for this in vain. Editor.
unreadable: no raised mark (e) found in the running text, where the note evidently belongs (item 4 line)

text: Sophronii esse non potest. Vid. infra Ang. Mai præfationem historiæ Cyri et Joannis. EDIT.
anchorLine: 9. In SS. quadraginta duos martyres (f) Amorienses, Latine in Bibl. concionatoria
en: It cannot be Sophronius's. See below Angelo Mai's preface to the history of Cyrus and John. Editor.

text: In ejusd. bibl. Taur. cod. 105, fol. 414, est ex Sophronii Synodica, cap. 35, De hæreticis atque hæresiarchis; atque in cod. 271, fol. 76, Sophronii De interpunctione. V. Cat. cit. pag. 198 et 375. HARL.
anchorLine: V. Cat. codd. Gr. Taur. p. 92 et 402 (g). Florentiæ, in bibl. Laurent. Med. cod. 34.
en: In the same Turin library, codex 105, fol. 414, there is an extract from Sophronius's Synodica, ch. 35, On heretics and heresiarchs; and in codex 271, fol. 76, Sophronius's On punctuation. See the cited Catalogue, pp. 198 and 375. Harles.
